Protocol

Bacterial phylogenomic surveillance

Determine how bacterial isolates are related to one another from whole-genome SNP phylogenies, for cluster detection and outbreak investigation.

Bacteria

This protocol compares whole genomes to measure relatedness between isolates. It is distinct from gene-targeted surveillance, such as detecting and tracking antimicrobial resistance genes. Bacteria recombine frequently, so the core SNP alignment is filtered for recombination before the final tree is built.

Helps answer

  • Are these cases related to each other?
  • When did this outbreak start, or when was the pathogen introduced?
  • Was this introduced once, or several times?
  • Is drug resistance spreading between cases? used with another protocol

Starting inputs

Raw reads, Reference genome, Collection dates

Steps

Choose a method at each step. Later steps only offer methods whose required inputs are produced by your earlier choices.

  1. 1

    Read preprocessing

    Remove adapters, primers, and low-quality sequence so downstream steps work from clean reads.

    Specified method

    • Details

      Trim adapter sequence and low-quality bases from reads.

      Needs Raw reads → Produces Clean reads

  2. 2

    Site masking Optional

    Exclude genomic regions whose variation would mislead downstream comparison.

    Recommended for most bacterial references.

    Specified methods (select one or more)

    These methods can be combined. Selected methods are applied in the order listed, and a method can use the output of one selected above it.

    • Details

      Mask prophages, insertion sequences, and other mobile elements in a bacterial reference.

      Needs Reference genome → Produces Mask regions

      Use when

      • The organism is a bacterium whose genomes carry prophages, insertion sequences, or other horizontally acquired elements.
      • You want SNP distances and trees to reflect the chromosome's clonal history.

      Combine with

      • Repeat and paralog masking: Add it when the reference also contains repeats such as rRNA operons or duplicated genes, which cause ambiguous read mapping.
      • Custom masking: Add your own BED file for species-specific regions that prediction tools do not find.

    • Details

      Mask repetitive and duplicated regions of a reference so reads cannot map ambiguously.

      Needs Reference genome → Produces Mask regions

      Use when

      • The genome contains gene families, duplicated genes, or other repeats, as is common in fungi.
      • Variant calls cluster in regions with unusually high or uneven coverage.

      Combine with

      • Mobile element masking: Add it for bacteria, whose horizontally transferred elements are not necessarily repeated in the reference.
      • Custom masking: Add your own BED file for species-specific regions that prediction tools do not find.

    • Details

      Mask regions you define yourself in a BED file, such as genes known to be unreliable for your species.

      Needs Reference genome → Produces Mask regions

      Use when

      • Published analyses of your species exclude specific genes or regions, such as PE/PPE genes in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
      • Your own data show regions with consistently poor coverage, mapping quality, or excess variant calls.
      • You need to reproduce another lab's analysis exactly, using the same mask they used.

      Skip this method when

      • The regions can be found reproducibly with a prediction tool, which is easier to rerun when the reference changes.

      Combine with

      • Mobile element masking: Use both when you have species-specific regions in addition to predicted mobile elements.
      • Repeat and paralog masking: Use both when you have species-specific regions in addition to repeats found by self-alignment.

    • Continue without this step. Later steps can't use anything it would have produced.

  3. 3

    Genome assembly and variant calling

    Reconstruct each sample's genome, or the differences between samples, from its sequencing reads.

    For the reference-based approach, choose a closed reference genome from the same lineage as the isolates where possible.

    Specified methods (choose one)

    • Details

      Map reads to a reference, call SNPs, and combine samples into a core SNP alignment of positions present in every sample.

      Needs Clean reads, Reference genome → Produces Full genome alignment, SNP-only alignment

      Use when

      • The genome is large, as with bacteria and fungi, and differences between samples are mostly SNPs.
      • A closed reference from the same lineage as your samples is available.
      • A later step needs genome positions, such as recombination filtering or reporting variants by reference coordinate.
      • You need reproducible SNP distances for outbreak or cluster definitions.

      Use another method when

      • Indels are informative and genomes are small enough to compare in full, as with most viruses. Use Reference-based consensus calling instead.
      • No closely related reference exists, or samples span lineages diverse enough that much of each genome fails to map. Use Reference-free SNP calling instead.
      • The organism is diploid and no ploidy-aware caller is used, since heterozygous sites will be miscalled.

    • Details

      Identify SNPs shared across samples directly from split k-mers, without a reference genome.

      Needs Clean reads → Produces SNP-only alignment

      Use when

      • No suitable reference genome exists for your samples.
      • Samples span lineages diverse enough that a single reference would introduce mapping bias.
      • You need fast SNP distances for screening or a first look at a new collection.

      Use another method when

      • A later step needs genome positions, such as recombination filtering, because only variable sites are kept. Use Reference-based SNP calling instead.
      • Indels carry signal you want to keep. Use Reference-based consensus calling instead.

  4. 4

    Recombination filtering Optional

    Identify and remove variation introduced by recombination so the remaining signal reflects vertical descent.

    Strongly recommended for most bacterial species. Skipping is reasonable only for largely clonal species with little recombination.

    Specified method

    • Details

      Alternate between tree building and detecting regions of elevated SNP density until the result converges.

      Needs Full genome alignment → Produces Recombination-filtered alignment, Phylogenetic tree

    • Continue without this step. Later steps can't use anything it would have produced.

  5. 5

    Phylogenetic inference

    Reconstruct the evolutionary relationships among samples from an alignment.

    Specified methods (select one or more)

    These methods can be combined. Selected methods are applied in the order listed, and a method can use the output of one selected above it.

    • Details

      Find the tree that best explains the alignment under a substitution model, with branch lengths in substitutions per site.

      Needs Recombination-filtered alignment or Full genome alignment or SNP-only alignment → Produces Phylogenetic tree

      Use when

      • You need a tree for clustering, population structure, or placing new samples. This is the default choice.
      • Collection dates are missing or unreliable.
      • You want a fast result with branch support values, even for thousands of genomes.

      Combine with

      • Time-scaled phylogeny: Apply it afterward to convert this tree's branch lengths into time when collection dates are available.

    • Details

      Rescale an existing tree, usually a maximum likelihood tree, so branch lengths are in time and ancestral nodes are dated.

      Needs Phylogenetic tree, Collection dates → Produces Time-scaled tree

      Use when

      • You need dates for events, such as introductions, common ancestors, or transmission windows.
      • You already have a tree, such as a maximum likelihood tree, and accurate collection dates for most samples.
      • The dataset is too large for a full Bayesian analysis, or results are needed quickly.

      Skip this method when

      • Dates are missing or imprecise, or a root-to-tip regression shows little temporal signal.
      • Samples were collected over a period too short for measurable evolution, so dates would be poorly constrained.
      • You need full uncertainty on the tree and dates, or phylodynamic estimates such as growth rates. Use Bayesian phylogeny instead.

      Combine with

      • Maximum likelihood phylogeny: Build the maximum likelihood tree first; this method takes it as input.
